title: Demonstrationes circa residua ex divisione potestatum per numeros primos resultantia

deep.reconstruction:
Context (Problem 34, previous page): for a prime P and an exponent n, count the 'proper cases' of x^n − 1. These are the residues x < P with P | x^n − 1 that do not already satisfy P | x^ν − 1 for some smaller exponent ν. In modern terms they are the residues of exact multiplicative order n mod P, or, in Euler's formal count, the primitive n-th roots of unity.

Solution on this page: the total number of cases for x^n − 1 is taken to be n. A lower formula x^ν − 1 is contained in x^n − 1 only when ν is an aliquot part (divisor) of n. To avoid excluding the same case twice, one subtracts only the cases proper to each such lower formula. This gives the recursion
  N(n) = n − Σ_{d|n, d<n} N(d),
which is equivalent to Σ_{d|n} N(d) = n.

Euler tabulates the recursion for n = 1,…,9:
- N(1) = 1
- N(2) = 2 − 1 = 1
- N(3) = 3 − 1 = 2
- N(4) = 4 − 1 − 1 = 2
- N(5) = 5 − 1 = 4
- N(6) = 6 − 2 − 1 − 1 = 2
- N(7) = 7 − 1 = 6
- N(8) = 8 − 2 − 1 − 1 = 4
- N(9) = 9 − 2 − 1 = 6

These are exactly φ(n). The page ends 'Hinc in genere si α, β, γ, δ etc. sint numeri primi, res ita se habebit:'. On the next page Euler generalizes by prime-power cases to N(α^λ β^μ γ^ν) = α^{λ−1}(α−1)β^{μ−1}(β−1)γ^{ν−1}(γ−1). He then observes that this equals the number of integers below n prime to n, i.e. his φ function from E271.

Purpose: this counting is the core of Euler's attempted proof that primitive roots exist mod P. Taking n = P − 1, all P − 1 cases are real (Coroll. 35, next page), so the proper cases of x^{P−1} − 1 are real too. Their number is φ(P−1) > 0.
errors: The count 'number of all cases = n' is the number of roots of x^n − 1 counted formally, possibly 'imaginary'. It is the actual number of residues only when n | P−1. The proof needs the fact that x^d − 1 has exactly d roots mod P for every d | P−1; this is the well-known weak point of Euler's primitive-root argument, which he tries to repair in Coroll. 35 and surrounding sections.
The general formula (next page) is obtained by induction from examples ('colligimus'), not proved. In particular the inclusion–exclusion pattern is not shown in general.
All arithmetic in the table on this page is correct.

ideas.what: Recursive count of 'proper' roots of x^n − 1 by subtracting the proper roots of x^d − 1 for each proper divisor d of n. This is equivalent to Σ_{d|n} N(d) = n.
ideas.modern_name: Divisor-sum identity Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n; counting elements of exact order d (primitive d-th roots of unity)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), art. 39 and arts. 52–55
ideas.where_published: E449 itself (Novi Commentarii 18, 1774); the totient was introduced in E271 (1763)

ideas.what: Identification of the number of proper cases with the number of integers less than n and prime to n.
ideas.modern_name: Number of primitive n-th roots of unity equals φ(n) (degree of the cyclotomic polynomial)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (φ); Gauss for the cyclotomic and primitive-root framework

missed.claim: Euler's recursion N(n) = n − Σ_{d|n, d<n} N(d), tabulated here, is in effect the identity Σ_{d|n} φ(d) = n, stated 27 years before Gauss. Standard histories (e.g. Dickson's History) tend to attribute this identity to Gauss. However, Euler's primitive-root proof in E449 is well known to historians, so this is at most a minor attribution nuance.
missed.quote: ne iidem casus bis vel pluries excludantur, tantum casus cuique proprii excludi debent, quo facto remanebunt casus formulae propositae x^n−1 proprii
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Attribution of the divisor-sum identity for φ; historical priority only, no new mathematics.

deep.surprise_reason: The content is Euler's well-documented (and gap-ridden) primitive-root argument in E449. The implicit Σφ(d) = n is a mild priority point, but the paper is standard in histories of primitive roots.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image. The Greek letter printed as a ϐ-form glyph is correctly rendered as β.
